stemMd: Which one of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: Because returned material sells for about twice the price of kerbside material, the scheme will become cheaper to run as returns rise.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Ostria's scheme has sharply raised returns, but its funding leans partly on the failures it is reducing and on an unpredictable commodity price.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Ostria's experience shows that a deposit of fifteen cents is enough to more than double the share of drinks containers that are recycled.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Deposit-return schemes ought not to be funded from unclaimed deposits at all, because an operator funded that way has a reason to discourage returns.

explanationMd:
A main-point answer must cover the whole passage and must claim no more than the author does. Trace the movement of the four paragraphs: the scheme raised returns from about 40 to 88 per cent; it is paid for partly by unclaimed deposits; that income falls as the scheme succeeds, which raises concerns; the planners' reply makes the outcome depend on the price of recycled plastic, a market nobody in Ostria controls.

The choice saying that the scheme has sharply raised returns but that its funding leans partly on the failures it is reducing and on an unpredictable commodity price follows all four steps: the success, the awkward funding source, and the dependence on the plastic price that the last paragraph ends on.

**How to check the answer.** Test each other choice against two questions. Does it cover more than one paragraph? Does the author actually assert it? The choice about the fifteen-cent deposit fails the first: it is the opening paragraph only. The choice about abolishing deposit funding and the choice predicting cheaper running costs both fail the second: one turns the critics' concern into the author's recommendation, and the other states as certain an outcome the passage says "depends" on the price of plastic.

distractorRationale.d: The passage reports this concern as the critics' view and then gives the planners' reply; the author never recommends abandoning deposit funding. The choice turns a reported objection into the author's thesis and is too strong.
distractorRationale.c: This is a detail from the first paragraph. It leaves out the funding problem that the remaining three paragraphs are about, and "shows that a deposit... is enough" is a causal claim the passage does not make so firmly.
distractorRationale.a: This takes the planners' point and drops its qualification. The passage says that whether the recycler gain outweighs the deposit loss "depends on the price of recycled plastic", so it does not predict that the scheme will become cheaper to run.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying passage on Ostria's deposit-return scheme. It asks which choice best expresses the main point of the passage. The four choices, in the order shown, are: deposit-return schemes ought not to be funded from unclaimed deposits at all, because an operator funded that way has a reason to discourage returns; Ostria's experience shows that a deposit of fifteen cents is enough to more than double the share of drinks containers that are recycled; Ostria's scheme has sharply raised returns, but its funding leans partly on the failures it is reducing and on an unpredictable commodity price; because returned material sells for about twice the price of kerbside material, the scheme will become cheaper to run as returns rise.

provenance.notes: Original main-point item on the original passage bocconi-ug-stim-deposit-return-546. Distractors are a single-paragraph detail, a reported objection promoted to thesis, and the planners' argument with its qualification removed.

review.author: bocconi-ug-wave8-verbal-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The passage notes the success in returns, then the awkward reliance on unclaimed deposits, then the dependence on a volatile commodity price, which is option B. 'Will become cheaper' overstates the planners' reply, which the passage leaves uncertain. 'Deposits ought not to fund schemes' is a prescription the author never makes. The fifteen-cent doubling point is a detail, and the 40% figure refers to kerbside collection. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-bocug-verbal-run1) reached the same answer: The passage reports higher returns, the awkward reliance on unclaimed deposits, and dependence on volatile recyclate prices, which is what the chosen option says. 'Will become cheaper as returns rise' ignores the stated uncertainty. 'Fifteen cents more than doubles recycling' is only a detail. 'Ought not to be funded from deposits at all' is a normative claim the passage never makes.]
